segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What was to do or to make in Spanish?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say it does or it makes?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now hace you can use like "ago". Like in English when you say "two weeks ago", you can say "it makes two weeks" in Spanish, and you get that meaning.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So week is semana. Two is... do you remember two?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Dos. So two weeks ago, you would say it makes two weeks.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Hace dos semanas. I saw him two weeks ago.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Lo vi hace dos semanas. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: To respond is responder. Responder. How would you say I responded?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Respondí. How would you say I responded to her?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: La respondí. No, le. Le respondí.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Le respondí. I responded to her. I responded to her seven weeks ago. Do you remember how to say seven, related to September?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Siete. Good. So I responded to her seven weeks ago.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Le respondí hace siete semanas.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now in Spanish you can say "I responded her it". For example, I responded to her letter, or I responded to her mail. Instead of saying it this way, to her mail, in Spanish you can just say I responded him the mail, I responded her the mail, or if you know what you're talking about, I responded him it, I responded her it. This is because, and something we will look at again later, Spanish does not use possessive words as much as English does. So it would be much more natural in Spanish "I responded her the mail", "I responded him the mail", instead of "I responded to her mail". So how would you say "I responded her it", which isn't great English, and it's perfect Spanish?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Se lo respondí. So the se is actually le, to her, the lo is el mail, and you get se lo respondí. I responded to her the mail. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: It's a masculine word, so how would you say the month?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And how would you say a month, or one month?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Un mes. So un mes can be a month or one month. So how would you say I responded it to her one month ago? I responded to her mail, I responded her it, one month ago.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Se lo respondí hace un mes.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Se lo respondí hace un mes. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we have respondí, I responded, how would you say he, she, it, you formal responded?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Respondimos. So respondí, respondió, respondimos. Let's make a quick recap with an -ar verb. How would you say discrimination?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: In English we say discrimination or descrimination?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Dis- oh, dis- it's with an "i", yeah.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Discriminé. He or she or it, you formal, discriminated?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So we have two more people to learn for the point in the past: they, and you informal. Let's begin with you informal.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: For you informal, in the point in the past, we have -aste for -ar verbs, and -iste for -er, -ir verbs. -aste for -ar verbs, and -iste for -er, -ir verbs.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how would you say you spoke, speaking informally?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Hablaste. And you ate, speaking informally?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No comiste? Didn't you eat it?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No lo comiste? Good. What was to leave or to go out?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Salir. How would you say did you go out, did you leave?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Saliste? Good. You didn't go out last night? Last night is anoche. Anoche.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now if you translate "tonight" directly, what you would come up with is anoche. So you must be careful not to get confused here. How do you say tonight in Spanish?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Esta noche, this night. So anoche is last night, not tonight. So how would you say did you go out last night, speaking informally?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Saliste anoche? Didn't you go out last night?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. No saliste anoche? What was to live?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Vivir. And how do you say where?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Dónde viviste? Where were you living?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Dónde vivías? So in many cases both line and point are perfectly fine. Dónde viviste, dónde vivías. All that means is that the speaker has two different ideas in their mind. Maybe you go abroad to study, and I will tell you dónde viviste, or maybe I will tell you dónde vivías.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Dónde viviste: where did you live, in this idea in my mind which is this closed amount of time. Where were you living, just means the idea in my mind is an ongoing idea of time. So many times it's completely interchangeable. What was to wait?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Esperar. Esperar. So for you informal, we have -aste for the point in the past. So how would you say you waited, speaking informally?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Esperaste. Good. Did you wait for me?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Me esperaste? Didn't you wait for me?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Why didn't you wait for me?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. ¿Por qué no me esperaste? What was to arrive?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Llegar. Good. How would you say when did you arrive? When did you arrive, informally?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. ¿Cuándo llegaste? This is an example of when you would need the point, because you probably wouldn't want to say when were you arriving, no? So here it's very strongly the point in time: when did you arrive, cuándo llegaste.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we have -aste and -iste for you informal. For they, we have -aron for -ar verbs, and -ieron for -er, -ir verbs. So how would you say they spoke? They spoke.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Lo prepararon. Good. We have -aron for -ar verbs, and -ieron, i-e-r-o-n, for -er, -ir verbs. How would you say they ate?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Comieron. They left, they went out?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So let's have a quick review of the panorama of this point in the past with hablar and comer, which we might want to use as our hooks. So we will begin with hablar. How do you say I spoke?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Hablaron. Good. Hablé, habló, hablamos, hablaste, hablaron. Now let's do the same for comer, so for -er, -ir verbs. How do you say I ate?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Comí. He, she, it, you formal ate?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Comieron. So what's very interesting here is that for -er, -ir verbs, in the present we had "e" popping up everywhere, no? Vive, viven, vives, and just one "i", just one "i" sound, just one "i" popping up, vivimos. But everything else was "e" for -er, -ir verbs in the present. But in the past, for -er, -ir verbs, we have "i" dominating the stage. We have the "i", "ee" sound everywhere, and this time the letter "e", the "eh" sound, occupying only one space, popping up in only one place, which is -ieron. Comí, comió, comiste, comimos, comieron.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Which is the exact inverse of what happens in the present tense. We can see also a logic that crosses over between the -ar group and the -er, -ir group. For example, we have I spoke, how is it?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Habló. We saw that -er, -ir in this past point has a special affiliation to the "ee" sound, the "i", the letter "i". So whilst we have hablé for -ar verbs, for -er, -ir verbs, what do we have? How would we say I ate?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Comí. And whilst we have habló for -ar verbs, what do we have for -er, -ir verbs? How would you say he ate?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Comió. So it's like the -ar version but with that important "i" popping up again. We have for we spoke, what do we have?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Comimos. That important "i", the "i", the "ee" sound again. For you informal spoke, what do we have?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Comiste. You remembered the importance of that "i", comiste. They spoke?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Comieron. Again that important "i", and that "e" getting just one small look in in that dot in the past to remind us that this is -er, -ir group, not just -ir. Just as what happened the other way round in the present. Good.
